from: State concealed-carry permit requirement (YES = permit required)
per: law switch 0->1 (dropping the permit, 1->0, gives the opposite: about +10%)
rampNote: Effect grows roughly linearly to full size over about 10 years (DAW synthetic control: +13-15% at year 10). Moving from shall-issue to permitless is smaller and faster: about +7% violent crime in the first 12 months (Parker, JPAM, NIBRS monthly data). Use about -0.07 when the prior regime was shall-issue, -0.13 to -0.15 when it was may-issue.
anchor: Right-to-carry adoption raised aggregate violent crime 13-15% ten years after adoption (synthetic control, state panel through 2014); RAND rates evidence 'supportive' that shall-issue raises violent crime; permitless carry raised gun assaults 32% where a training requirement was lost (Doucette et al. 2024, CPP) and violent crime 7.3% in the first year (Parker, JPAM)
source: Donohue, Aneja & Weber 2019, Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 16(2):198-247
caveats: Contested by Moody & Marvell comments (Econ Journal Watch). Permitless-carry literature is newer and shorter-run. Effect concentrated in aggravated/gun assault.

from: State ends cash bail (YES = no money bail)
rampNote: No detectable aggregate change; any effect would show within 6-12 months of implementation.
anchor: New Jersey 2017 reform: money bail fell ~11 percentage points with about a 2-point rise in pretrial rearrest (MDRC interrupted time series) and no rise in firearm violence (synthetic control); New York 2020: no significant change in aggregate crime except robbery; Illinois 2023: violent crime fell about 6% in the following year (descriptive, Loyola CCJ)
source: Anderson, Redcross, Valentine & Miratrix 2019, MDRC 'Evaluation of Pretrial Justice System Reforms That Use the Public Safety Assessment: Effects of New Jersey's Criminal Justice Reform'
caveats: Reforms differ: NJ paired bail abolition with risk assessment and detention hearings. Illinois evidence is descriptive, not causal. NY robbery increase is the one positive signal.

from: State raises juvenile court age (YES = 17-year-olds in juvenile court)
rampNote: Cohort effect; if any, appears within 1-3 years as affected cohorts age through.
anchor: Connecticut raised the age of majority 16->17 (2010) and 17->18 (2012): no statistically significant effect on crime or delinquency
caveats: Arora (Columbia working paper) argues deterrence at the age of majority is understated; Massachusetts raise-the-age raised recidivism for affected 17-year-olds (CPP 2022). Affected ages are a small share of state violent crime, so the state-level bound is tight either way.

from: State civilian oversight of police (YES = oversight board with power to investigate/discipline)
rampNote: City-level adoption; effect, if any, builds over several years. Sign depends on authority: investigate-and-sanction boards lower, review-only boards raise.
anchor: 217 US cities over 100,000 population, 1981-2015: broad-authority oversight agencies decreased violent crime and officer line-of-duty deaths; narrow-authority (review/audit only) agencies increased violent crime; magnitude not recovered
source: Ali & Nicholson-Crotty 2021, Public Performance & Management Review 44(3)
caveats: Single city panel with two-way fixed effects; no state-level design; magnitude unknown. A state mandate is not the same as a local board.

rampNote: Short-run bumps at legalization, no long-run shift.
anchor: Colorado and Washington vs synthetic/comparison states: no significant long-term effect on violent or property crime (Lu et al.); Washington-Oregon border difference-in-differences found reductions in rapes and property crime (Dragone et al. 2019)
source: Dragone, Prarolo, Vanin & Zanella 2019, Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 159:488-501
caveats: Dragone finds a decrease (rapes, thefts) but in a narrow border design; state-level synthetic control (Lu et al. 2019/2021, Justice Quarterly) finds none. Harper & Jorgensen 2023 similar null.

rampNote: Low-level offense reports fall within months; violent crime unchanged.
anchor: Denver STAR pilot: reports of less-serious crimes fell 34% in served precincts; no increase and no measurable change in violent crime
caveats: Six-month pilot, 8 precincts. The 34% applies to low-level offenses (trespass, disorder), not the violent crime rate. Good candidate for a separate low-level-offense or arrests outcome.

from: Mandatory minimum sentences in force (YES = mandatory minimums)
rampNote: Deterrence on repeat offenders appears within 1-3 years; incapacitation margin is near zero at current US incarceration levels.
anchor: California three-strikes cut felony arrests 17-20% among offenders with two strikes (a small population); Roodman's review concludes decarceration at today's margins has about zero net effect on crime
source: Roodman 2017, Open Philanthropy Project 'The Impacts of Incarceration on Crime'
caveats: Helland & Tabarrok 2007 (Journal of Human Resources 42(2)) is the main deterrence anchor but judged costly per crime averted. Reducing minimums is the mirror (size +0.01 per repeal).

from: State Housing First as the rule for homelessness funding
rampNote: Population effect comes through added permanent supportive housing beds over 2-5 years; mostly on chronic/unsheltered counts.
anchor: Individual RCTs (Pathways, At Home/Chez Soi) show large housing-stability gains, but community panels find modest effects: Corinth 2017 (all US CoCs 2007-2014) finds a small reduction in the homeless count per added PSH bed with heavy offset; Byrne et al. 2014 find modest negative associations with chronic homelessness
caveats: Exact per-bed number not verified from the paper (recalled as roughly 0.1 fewer homeless per bed). Evans, Phillips & Ruffini 2021 (JPAM 40(3):914-963) stress individual-level evidence and gaps at population level. Utah chronic claims were revised.

from: Federal housing vouchers for every eligible family
rampNote: Lease-up takes 1-3 years; full effect around 36 months. Largest on family and sheltered counts.
anchor: Family Options Study RCT: families offered a long-term subsidy had less than half as many subsequent homelessness episodes and substantially fewer shelter stays at 3 years than usual care
source: Gubits, Shinn, Wood et al. 2016, HUD Office of Policy Development and Research, Family Options Study: 3-Year Impacts
caveats: The RCT is individual-level among families already in shelter; scaling to universal eligibility (about 8.2 million more households per CBPP/Urban) is an extrapolation with no measured population estimate. Singles with disabilities and unsheltered people respond less to vouchers alone; market rent effects could offset.

from: Federal limits on power-plant carbon (2024 Carbon Pollution Standards type)
rampNote: Compliance dates 2030-2032; effect phases in over 6-8 years after finalization.
anchor: EPA RIA: up to 4,500 premature deaths avoided in 2032 (PM2.5 and ozone). Coal-plant PM2.5 averaged only 0.07 µg/m³ nationally in 2020, down from 2.34 in 1999 (Henneman et al. 2023 Science), so today's residual power-sector PM2.5 is a small share of a ~7-8 µg/m³ average. Derived estimate: 0.02-0.1 µg/m³, i.e. -0.3% to -1.3%.
source: US EPA 2024, Regulatory Impact Analysis for the Carbon Pollution Standards (EPA-452/R-24-009)
caveats: The proportional PM2.5 figure is my conversion, not a number EPA reports. Driscoll et al. 2015 (Nature Climate Change) found about 3,500 deaths/yr avoided for a strong option when coal was larger; the effect has shrunk since. EPA published a partial-repeal RIA in September 2026. Much larger in coal-heavy states (WV, KY, WY).

rampNote: Emission cuts appear 5-9 years after enactment as the standard ramps.
anchor: Difference-in-differences: 5-9 years after enactment, states with stringent ('clean') RPS cut power-sector SO2 57.6% and NOx 33.7%; weak designs cut SO2 25% and NOx not at all. LBNL retrospective: existing RPS cut national SO2/NOx/PM2.5 emissions about 5% and yielded about $5.2 billion/yr in health benefits
source: Ji, Li, Lee, Luke & Mavrothalassitis 2024, SSRN working paper 'Cleaner Bills, Cleaner Air'
caveats: Emission cuts are not concentration cuts: power-sector sulfate is now a small share of PM2.5 and crosses state lines. Proportional PM2.5 figure is derived. Working paper, not peer-reviewed; Wiser et al. 2017 (Environmental Research Letters) is the peer-reviewed benefits estimate.

rampNote: Facility co-pollutant cuts of 3-9% per year after start; concentration effect small.
anchor: California cap-and-trade lowered PM2.5, PM10 and NOx emissions of regulated industrial facilities 3-9% per year in 2012-2017 and narrowed the environmental-justice gap 21-30%; RGGI 2009-2014 health co-benefits valued at $3-8.3 billion (Manion et al. 2017, modeled)
source: Hernandez-Cortes & Meng 2023, Journal of Public Economics 217:104786
caveats: Facility emissions, not statewide ambient concentration. Perera et al. 2020 (EHP) RGGI child-health benefits are BenMAP modeling, not causal. Leakage to neighboring states reduces the net effect.

anchor: Instrumented state panel 1971-1997: large effects on property crime (1 point of unemployment -> about 2.1% burglary, 1% auto theft), weak and mostly insignificant for violent crime. Gould et al.: wages matter more for violent crime (10% higher low-skill wages -> 10.8% less violent crime)
source: Raphael & Winter-Ebmer 2001, Journal of Law and Economics 44(1):259-283
caveats: The game's +1% assault per point sits at the upper-middle of a range whose lower end is zero. Gould, Weinberg & Mustard 2002 (Review of Economics and Statistics) suggest wages are the stronger lever.

rampNote: Accelerates once median rent exceeds about 32% of median income (Glynn, Byrne & Culhane).
anchor: A $100 rise in median rent was associated with 15% more homelessness in metro areas and 39% in suburban/rural areas (2009 HUD data); Hanratty 2017 finds rent is the only local condition that stays significant with area fixed effects
source: Byrne, Munley, Fargo, Montgomery & Culhane 2013, Journal of Urban Affairs 35(5)
caveats: Cross-sectional/fixed-effects association, not a natural experiment. Conversion from $100 to 10% assumes a median rent near $800-1,000. Eviction causal anchor: Collinson et al. 2024 (QJE, judge leniency IV) find an eviction order raises individual homelessness and shelter use, magnitude not recovered. Colburn & Aldern 2022 is descriptive.

rampNote: Homelessness lags job loss by about a year; evictions follow job loss by up to two years (Collinson et al.).
anchor: Each 1-point rise in unemployment associated with about 0.65 more homeless people per 10,000 (Corinth-based model, 2007-2009), roughly 3% of a ~20 per 10,000 base; Hanratty 2017 finds unemployment loses significance with area fixed effects
caveats: The 0.65 figure comes from a secondary source (Community Solutions/O'Flaherty summary) and was not verified in Corinth's paper. PIT counts barely rose in the Great Recession; the effect is likely near zero in the short run.
